problem: Model-based long-horizon navigation in partial maps (LSP) only assigns an exploration cost to revealing unseen space and ignores the value of the information revealed, so robots do not go out of their way to gather performance-critical information such as a map room. Belief-space planning that would capture this is intractable, and end-to-end RL lacks completeness.
motivation: In large unseen buildings, a detour to reveal informative space (e.g., a map) can save much more travel cost than it costs. Quantifying that long-horizon value of information is hard since it depends on how behavior changes over a whole deployment across all possible unseen configurations, so a tractable training-time way to compute and learn it is needed.
key_idea: Compute a per-frontier long-horizon value of information at training time as the summed one-step cost-to-go difference between an LSP policy with and without the region revealed, learn to predict it with a GNN, and subtract it from the exploration cost in the LSP planning objective.
insight: Because the planner subtracts a learned V_I from the exploration cost, it discovers from training data alone that revealing the map room is valuable, without being told such a room exists. The value is context-dependent: in the trial where the robot starts next to the goal, it heads toward the map room but turns back when the cost outweighs the benefit. Gains are largest in environments where key information is hidden and dead ends are many (Ring Office), and smaller in Parallel Hallway.
method: LSP abstraction: high-level actions are frontier subgoals with learned properties P_S, R_S, R_E; planning is sound and complete because the robot always moves through known space.
Value-of-information-augmented objective: Q adds -V_I(a_t) inside the failure branch alongside R_E, so information-rich frontiers become cheaper to explore.

Training-time V_I computation: one-step v_I is the difference in cost-to-go under the known map between the LSP policy on the partial map m_t and on m_t ∪ a_t; V_I is the sum of v_I over the remaining trajectory.

GNN estimator: a GATv2Conv graph network on a sparse map graph (7-d node features: semantic one-hot, neighbor count, subgoal and goal flags; edge feature: geodesic distance) predicts P_S, R_S, R_E and V_I per subgoal node; P_S is trained with cross-entropy.
Data generation: offline trials with the base LSP planner alternating with an optimistic planner for diversity; labels come from the underlying known map; hundreds of trials per training environment.

setting.backbone: GNN with GATv2Conv layers (trained from scratch) inside LSP model-based planner
setting.training_data: Simulated procedural maps: 200 Ring Office maps, 500 Parallel Hallway maps, with hundreds of trials per environment (J-Intersection count not stated)
setting.observation: Semantic planar laser scan building a partial semantic occupancy grid map plus robot pose
setting.action_space: High-level frontier subgoals executed via low-level motion primitives
setting.simulator: Custom procedural 2D office-like simulator (J-Intersection, Ring Office, Parallel Hallway)
setting.privileged: none at test time (the underlying known map is used only to generate training labels)

numbers.evidence: Table I: Avg. Cost over Multiple Trials in all Tested Environments, J-Intersection LSP-AIG 93.84

numbers_note: Results are average path cost (lower is better) in custom environments, not standard benchmarks. Baselines (non-learned, LSP-GNN, Map-seeker) are omitted here. Text reports improvements: J-Intersection 36.9% and 13.0%; Ring Office 63.76% and 36.68%; Parallel Hallway 10.62% and 11.33%.
results: LSP-AIG lowers average cost in all three environments, e.g., Ring Office 196.65 versus 310.57 for LSP-GNN and 542.64 for the non-learned baseline (63.76% and 36.68% improvements). In Parallel Hallway it reaches 228.11 versus 253.95 for LSP-GNN and 252.35 for the naive planner; the systematic Map-seeker scores 257.99. It always seeks the key information in J-Intersection.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulated, procedurally generated office-like environments with simple semantic-color inputs, with no real-robot tests
No ablations or comparison against end-to-end RL baselines; only three environments and a non-learned/LSP-GNN baseline set
V_I labels are approximate (summed one-step differences) and depend on the base LSP policy used to collect data
